name: Flower bowl shoes

lead: Flower bowl shoes, also called flowerpot shoes or Manchu platform shoes, were worn by Manchu women of the Qing dynasty (1644-1911). A fabric upper sat on a wooden platform under the arch, raising the wearer and giving the foot a small, delicate appearance.

The shoes were part of formal Manchu dress and were embroidered with flowers and auspicious motifs. Accounts differ on why the style arose: some say it echoed the gait of Han women with bound feet, while others point to northeastern living conditions.

paras: The wearer walked on the central wooden platform, with a short step and swaying gait. Variants include the flowerpot style, thick in the middle and tapering at toe and heel, and the horse-hoof style with a concave-sided block. Platforms are reported at roughly 5 to 15 cm.

Walking on a narrow central platform requires balance and shortens the stride. Padded soles are suggested to have made some pairs suitable for indoor or special-occasion wear. Unlike foot binding, which Manchu custom forbade, the shoes did not alter the foot.

chain: Taller, slimmer-looking silhouette with a small foot
angle.text: The raised sole adds height and visually shrinks the foot, which was part of the elegant look of Manchu court dress. The gait was shortened and swaying.

lead: Flower bowl shoes, known in Chinese as huapenxie (flowerpot shoes), are one of two high-platform styles of Manchu women's footwear (qixie) from the Qing dynasty, the other being matixie, horse-hoof shoes [1].

They look better-proportioned by adding height and making the foot appear small: a wooden platform sits under the arch with the toe and heel left near the ground, so the wearer stands taller and the foot reads as slender. Grokipedia reports platform heights of about 10 to 13 cm, and Wikipedia describes thick soles thinning toward toe and heel [1][2].

Wikipedia says the Manchu banned their women from foot binding. Some suggest the platforms imitated the gait of bound-foot women, while others attribute them to living conditions in the Northeast [1].

paras: The upper was fabric, often embroidered silk, and the platform wood. The sole was padded with cotton layers. Flowerpot shoes had thick soles that thinned at toe and heel; horse-hoof shoes used a wooden piece with concave sides attached to the sole. Left and right shoes were interchangeable [1].
Grokipedia describes embroidered motifs such as flowers, butterflies and goldfish, and platform heights varying with status and region [2].

Both styles appeared early in the Qing dynasty and were still worn in the late Qing. By the mid-19th century a Manchu woman's outfit included the platform shoes, the Manchu robe and the liangbatou headdress [1].

Folk stories attribute the shoes to a goddess avoiding mud and insects, or to a princess, Duoluo Ganzhu, whose soldiers used wooden stilts to cross marshes. Foot binding was practised by Han women and banned among Manchu; in the late Qing some Manchu women briefly adopted a loose binding called liutiaojiao [1].
Examples are held in museum collections including the Textile Museum at George Washington University and the Bata Shoe Museum [1].

timeline.event: Start of the Qing dynasty, in which the shoes appear in the early period [1].
End of the Qing dynasty; the shoes were worn into the late Qing [1][2].
